questions.q: What is Meridian Health Network, as this capstone frames it?
options: A single hospital that has always operated as one unified organization
A newly formed parent company consolidating three previously independent hospital systems under one ServiceNow instance
A software vendor Meridian is evaluating as a replacement for ServiceNow
A regulatory body overseeing healthcare IT standards
questions.explain: Meridian is the parent holding company formed when St. Catherine's, Lakeshore, and Prairie View agreed to consolidate under one corporate umbrella.

questions.q: Applying Chapter 2's test for a second production instance, why does Meridian NOT qualify for one per hospital system?
options: There's no data-residency requirement forcing physical separation, and the systems aren't truly independent — they'll share patients, corporate functions, and reporting
ServiceNow technically cannot support more than one hospital system per instance
Multi-instance architectures are always illegal under healthcare regulation
The three systems have identical HR systems already, so no integration work is needed
questions.explain: Chapter 2's two legitimate justifications — data residency and true independence — both fail here, even though the systems' historical autonomy is real.

questions.q: Why is Prairie View's eight-year-old failed consolidation relevant to this capstone's governance question?
options: It proves ServiceNow cannot work for rural hospital networks
It has no bearing on the current architecture decision
It means Prairie View should be excluded from the new instance entirely
It suggests the earlier failure was a governance failure — decisions imposed top-down with no mechanism for local input — not a technology failure
questions.explain: The lesson frames the past failure as evidence that governance, not technology, is the real risk this time — which is why Chapter 8's governance question has to be answered up front.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say the one-instance-plus-governance decision should become an Architecture Decision Record rather than just a kickoff-meeting conclusion?
options: An ADR replaces the need for any governance model at all
So the context, options considered, and reasoning survive past the people in that meeting, for when someone later questions the decision
Meeting notes are not permitted to be stored in ServiceNow
ADRs are a legal requirement for any healthcare organization
questions.explain: This directly applies Chapter 1's ADR discipline: without a durable written record, a sound decision is vulnerable to being second-guessed or reversed by someone who never knew the original constraints.

questions.q: What does the lesson identify as the real cost of building three siloed instances instead of one for Meridian?
options: ServiceNow charges less per instance as more instances are purchased
Chapter 2's maintenance multiplier applied three times over — three upgrade schedules, three security models, three sets of integration endpoints
There is no real cost difference between one instance and three for an organization this size
Three instances would actually be cheaper because each system already has its own IT staff
questions.explain: The lesson ties directly back to Chapter 2's upgrade/maintenance multiplier — every platform-wide responsibility repeats once per production instance.
